'''Sulamith Goldhaber''' ({{langx|he|שולמית גולדהבר}}; November 4, 1923 – December 11, 1965), {{Nee|Low}}, was a [[high-energy physics|high-energy physicist]] and [[molecular spectroscopy|molecular spectroscopist]].<ref name="BioWIS" />  Goldhaber was a world expert on the interactions of [[Kaon|K<sup>+</sup> mesons]] with [[nucleons]] and made numerous discoveries relating to it.<ref name="BioWIS" />

==Biography==
Sulamith Low was born November 4, 1923, in [[Vienna]], Austria.<ref name="LuisA" /><ref name="BioWIS" /> She grew up in [[Mandatory Palestine|Palestine]] after her family emigrated out of Austria.<ref name="LuisA" /> She attended [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]] where she met her future husband, [[Gerson Goldhaber]].<ref name="LuisA" /> She graduated with an M.Sc. in 1947, and was married to Gerson the same year.<ref name="LuisA" /> The Goldhabers moved to the United States to pursue doctorates at [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] which they were awarded in 1951.<ref name="LuisA" /><ref name="BioWIS" /> The couple with their son Amos Nathaniel moved to Columbia University in New York City, where Gerson worked in the physics department, and Sulamith, despite her degree in physical chemistry, found work as an assistant to [[Jack Steinberger]], working on what were then considered high energy experiments at the Nevis Laboratory of Columbia.

Goldhaber became a [[naturalized citizen]] of the United States in 1953.<ref name="BioWIS" /> The Goldhabers moved to [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]], [[California]], in 1953 when Gerson was given a job as an [[assistant professor]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California]].<ref name="LuisA" /> While Goldhaber had previously worked in [[physical chemistry]], she was able to transition to [[high energy physics]] and form a collaboration with her husband working on [[nuclear emulsion]].<ref name="LuisA" /> The Goldhabers hoped to use their nuclear emulsion technique with the newly opened [[Bevatron]]—at the time the highest energy accelerator in operation—and it was through their methods that they observed some of the earliest interactions between [[Kaon|K<sup>−</sup> mesons]] and [[protons]].<ref name="LuisA" /> Using the Bevatron and the nuclear emulsion technique Goldhaber was the first to observe mass splitting in charged E [[hyperon]]s as well as the first nuclear interactions of the [[antiproton]].<ref name="LuisA" />

In the 1960s the Goldhabers realized that they should begin using the [[bubble chamber]] to continue their studies instead of nuclear emulsion so they formed the "Goldhaber–Trilling Group" with [[George Trilling]].<ref name="LuisA" /><ref name="BioWIS" /> Goldhaber quickly became a renowned expert in hydrogen bubble chamber physics, accruing a lengthy list of invited papers and conference talks.<ref name="LuisA" /> The Goldhabers were the first to measure the spin of the [[Kaon|K* meson]] and the first to study the simultaneous production of pairs of resonant states.<ref name="LuisA" /><ref name="BioWIS" /> They also invented the [[triangle diagram]] to aid in their research.<ref name="LuisA" /><ref name="BioWIS" />
Early in this period, the Goldhabers were both [[Ford Foundation]] fellows at [[CERN]] where they co-authored a CERN report<ref>[https://cds.cern.ch/record/278084/files/p1.pdf Separation of high-energy particles by means of strong interaction processes, CERN-61-03]</ref> together with B. Peters.

Goldhaber was in high demand as a speaker at scientific conferences due to her mastery of her field, and her ability to express herself beautifully.<ref name="LuisA" /> She gave a seminal talk on the production and interaction of heavy [[Meson|mesons]] and [[Hyperon|hyperons]] at the 1956 [[International Conference on High Energy Physics|Rochester Conference]] that marked the transition from [[cosmic ray]] based experiments to [[particle accelerator]] base experiments in the study of [[Strange quark|strange]] particles.<ref>{{cite archive|first=|last=|item=Program for the Sixth Annual Conference on High Energy Nuclear Physics|item-url=|type=|item-id=|date=|page=|pages=|fonds=|series=Sixth Annual Rochester Conference on High Energy Nuclear Physics – Rochester, New York|file=|box=Box 1, Folder 71 – Scientific program – Advisory board, tentative programs|collection=Robert E. Marshak Papers|collection-url=https://ead.lib.virginia.edu/vivaxtf/view?docId=oai/lib.vt.edu/repositories/2/resources/3579.oai_ead.xml|repository=|institution=Special Collections and University Archives, Virginia Tech|location=|oclc=|accession=}}</ref><ref name="LuisA" /> In the fall of 1965 the Goldhabers took a [[sabbatical]] to travel around the world visiting high energy laboratories and giving lectures.<ref name="LuisA" /> They first stopped at [[Oxford]] for the biennial European conference on high energy physics, and then [[CERN]] so that Goldhaber could discuss methods of making automatic film measurements with Berkeley's [[Hough-Powell device]].<ref name="LuisA" /> The Goldhabers then traveled to [[Ankara]] to lecture, and spent a month at the [[Weizmann Institute]] in preparation for the lectures Sulamith was to give in [[Madras]], India.<ref name="LuisA" />

In Madras Goldhaber suffered a [[stroke]].<ref name="LuisA" /> [[Exploratory surgery]] revealed a growing [[brain tumor]].<ref name="LuisA" /><ref name="BioWIS" /> She died without having regained consciousness on December 11, 1965.<ref name="LuisA" /><ref name="BioWIS" />

Goldhaber had one son with her husband named [[Nat Goldhaber|Amos]].<ref name="CV">{{cite web|url=http://cwp.library.ucla.edu/Phase2/Goldhaber,_Sulamith@812345678.html|title= Sulamith Goldhaber|access-date= 2008-04-28|publisher= University of California, Los Angeles}}</ref> She was remembered by her friends and colleagues as "a distinguished scientist, a remarkable homemaker and hostess, and a devoted wife and mother".<ref name="LuisA" />
